The **Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty** (**CTBT**) is a [multilateral treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multilateral_treaty "Multilateral treaty") to ban [nuclear weapons test](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_test "Nuclear weapons test") explosions and any other [nuclear explosions](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_explosions "Nuclear explosions"), for both civilian and military purposes, in all environments. It was adopted by the [United Nations General Assembly](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") on 10 September 1996, but has not [entered into force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_into_force "Coming into force"), as it has not been ratified by all the required states. The treaty will establish the [Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty_Organization "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization") to oversee monitoring, which is currently done by a [Preparatory Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preparatory_Commission_for_the_Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty_Organization "Preparatory Commission for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization").

Despite not being in force, the CTBT has established a global norm against nuclear testing, reinforced by nuclear testing moratoria declared by the five nuclear-weapon states recognized under the [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_the_Non-Proliferation_of_Nuclear_Weapons "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") (NPT): [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_China "Nuclear weapons of China"), [France](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "France and weapons of mass destruction"), [Russia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Russia and weapons of mass destruction"), the [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_the_United_Kingdom "Nuclear weapons of the United Kingdom"), and the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_of_the_United_States "Nuclear weapons of the United States"). Since the treaty's opening for signature in 1996, only sixteen nuclear tests have been conducted, all by non-signatory states: [Pokhran-II](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokhran-II "Pokhran-II") by India and [Chagai-I](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chagai-I "Chagai-I") by Pakistan in May 1998, and [six tests by North Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_weapons_tests_of_North_Korea "List of nuclear weapons tests of North Korea") from [2006](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_North_Korean_nuclear_test "2006 North Korean nuclear test") to [2017](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_North_Korean_nuclear_test "2017 North Korean nuclear test"). Over 2,000 nuclear tests were conducted between 1945 and 1996, primarily by the United States and the [Soviet Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Soviet Union and weapons of mass destruction").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The CTBT's [International Monitoring System](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monitoring_System "International Monitoring System") is a global [nuclear detonation detection system](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_detonation_detection_system "Nuclear detonation detection system"). It is intended to comprise 321 monitoring stations and 16 laboratories across 89 countries, of which ~90% are already operational. The stations collect one of [seismic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seismic_wave "Seismic wave"), [infrasonic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrasound "Infrasound"), [hydroacoustic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroacoustic "Hydroacoustic"), and [radionuclide](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fallout "Nuclear fallout") signatures of nuclear explosions. The IMS successfully characterized all six North Korean nuclear tests, and also collects [large datasets](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_data "Big data") valuable to scientists for [astrophysics](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrophysics "Astrophysics"), [biology](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology"), and [geology](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology "Geology") and more.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

As of 2026, [188 states have signed and 179 states have ratified the treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_parties_to_the_Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty "List of parties to the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty"). The treaty designates a "Annex 2" list of states, which must all ratify the CTBT for it to enter into force. These states possessed any [nuclear reactors](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactors "Nuclear reactors") at the time. Nine Annex 2 states have yet to ratify: the six signatories China, [Egypt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Egypt and weapons of mass destruction"), Iran, Israel, Russia, and the United States, and the three non-signatories India, Pakistan, and North Korea. Israel is also [widely believed to possess nuclear weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons_and_Israel "Nuclear weapons and Israel"), and the [nuclear program of Iran](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran "Nuclear program of Iran") is heavily scrutinized internationally.

The CTBT was negotiated in 1995-96 in the [Conference on Disarmament](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_on_Disarmament "Conference on Disarmament") with a final phase of negotiations in the UN General Assembly. It built on two major previous treaties, the 1963 [Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty "Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty") and the 1968 NPT, as well as the 1974 [Threshold Test Ban Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threshold_Test_Ban_Treaty "Threshold Test Ban Treaty") between the US and Soviet Union limiting the yields of their underground tests to less than 150 [kilotons of TNT](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilotons_of_TNT "Kilotons of TNT").

While the United States was the first nation to sign the CTBT, the [United States Senate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") rejected ratification in 1999. In 2023, in the context of the [Russo-Ukrainian war](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022–present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)"), Russia withdrew its ratification of the CTBT. Non-ratifying states typically explain their reasoning via the non-ratification of a rival, or other regional stability issues.[[3]](#cite_note-l864-3)

The movement for international control of [nuclear weapons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") began in 1945, with a call from Canada and the United Kingdom for a conference on the subject.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPolsby198456-4) In June 1946, [Bernard Baruch](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Baruch "Bernard Baruch"), an emissary of President [Harry S. Truman](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman"), proposed the [Baruch Plan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baruch_Plan "Baruch Plan") before the [United Nations Atomic Energy Commission](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Atomic_Energy_Commission "United Nations Atomic Energy Commission"), which called for an international system of controls on the production of atomic energy. The plan, which would serve as the basis for U.S. nuclear policy into the 1950s, was rejected by the [Soviet Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") as a US ploy to cement its nuclear dominance.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStrode19907-5)[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPolsby198457–58-6)

Between the [Trinity nuclear test](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test) "Trinity (nuclear test)") of 16 July 1945 and the signing of the [Partial Test Ban Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_Test_Ban_Treaty "Partial Test Ban Treaty") (PTBT) on 5 August 1963, 499 nuclear tests were conducted.[[7]](#cite_note-delcoigne

| Type | [Strategic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_nuclear_weapon "Strategic nuclear weapon") [nuclear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") [disarmament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament") |

**New START**[[c]](#cite_note-5) was a [nuclear arms reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_disarmament "Nuclear disarmament") [treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty") between the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") with the formal name of ***Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms***. It was signed on 8 April 2010 in [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague"),[[3]](#cite_note-Lee-6)[[4]](#cite_note-7) and after [ratification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratification "Ratification")[[5]](#cite_note-csmonitor.com-8)[[6]](#cite_note-af.reuters.com-9) it [entered into force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entry_into_force "Entry into force") on 5 February 2011.[[1]](#cite_note-USA_Today/The_Associated_Press-1)

New START replaced the Treaty of [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") ([SORT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SORT "SORT")), which was to expire in December 2012. It followed the [START I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_I "START I") treaty, which expired in December 2009; the proposed [START II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_II "START II") treaty which never entered into force; and the [START III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_III "START III") treaty, for which negotiations were never concluded.

The treaty called for halving the number of [strategic nuclear missile launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile "Intercontinental ballistic missile"). It also called for the establishment of a new inspection and verification regime, replacing the SORT mechanism. It did not limit the number of operationally inactive [nuclear warheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_stockpile "Nuclear stockpile") that can be stockpiled, a number in the high thousands.[[7]](#cite_note-10)

On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START.[[8]](#cite_note-11) However, it did not withdraw from the treaty, and clarified that it would continue to abide by the numerical limits in the treaty.[[9]](#cite_note-12)[[10]](#cite_note-230221_suspension_nhk-13)[[11]](#cite_note-14) On 5 February 2026, the treaty officially expired.[[12]](#cite_note-RBK-15)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/New_START.ogv/250px-seek%3D85-New_START.ogv.jpg)](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d1/New_START.ogv)

Signing the New START Treaty (video in Russian)

The treaty limited the number of [deployed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_deployment#Nuclear_weapons "Military deployment") strategic [nuclear warheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warhead "Nuclear warhead") for each party to 1,550, which was down nearly two-thirds from the [original START treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_I "START I"), as well as 10% lower than the deployed strategic warhead limit of the 2002 Moscow Treaty.[[13]](#cite_note-O'Hanlon-16) The total number of deployed warheads could exceed the 1,550 limit by a few hundred because only one warhead is counted per bomber regardless of how many it actually carries.[[13]](#cite_note-O'Hanlon-16) The treaty also limited the number of deployed and non-deployed [intercontinental ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile "Intercontinental ballistic missile") (ICBM) launchers, [submarine-launched ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine-launched_ballistic_missile "Submarine-launched ballistic missile") (SLBM) launchers, and [heavy bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_bomber "Heavy bomber") equipped for nuclear armaments to 800. The number of deployed ICBMs, SLBMs, and heavy bombers equipped for nuclear armaments was limited to 700.[[14]](#cite_note-17) The treaty allowed for satellite and remote monitoring, as well as 18 on-site inspections per year to verify limits.[[13]](#cite_note-O'Hanlon-16)

Summary of New START limits[[15]](#cite_note-18)

| Type | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Deployed missiles and bombers | 700 |
| Deployed warheads ([MIRVs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_independently_targetable_reentry_vehicle "Multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle") and bombers) | 1,550 |
| Deployed and non-deployed launchers (missile tubes and bombers) | 800 |

The obligations had to be met within seven years from the date the treaty entered into force. The treaty was set to last ten years, with an option to renew it for up to five years upon the agreement of both parties.[[16]](#cite_note-19) The treaty entered into force on 5 February 2011, when the United States and Russia exchanged instruments of ratification, following approval by the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senate "U.S. Senate") and the [Federal Assembly of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Assembly_of_Russia "Federal Assembly of Russia").[[17]](#cite_note-20) The United States began implementing the reductions before the treaty was ratified.[[18]](#cite_note-21)

Documents made available to the U.S. Senate described[*[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] removal from service of at least 30 missile silos, 34 bombers, and 56 submarine launch tubes. Missiles which were removed would stay intact, and bombers could be converted to conventional use. Four of the twenty-four launchers on each of the [fourteen ballistic missile nuclear submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio-class_submarine "Ohio-class submarine") would be removed, and none retired.[[19]](#cite_note-22)

The treaty placed no limits on [tactical systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_nuclear_weapon "Tactical nuclear weapon").[[20]](#cite_note-23) In July 2010, Rebecca Grant for *[Air & Space Forces Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_&_Space_Forces_Magazine "Air & Space Forces Magazine")* reported that no limit was placed on the [Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_F-35_Lightning_II "Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II"), which would most likely be replacing the F-15E and F-16 in the tactical nuclear delivery role.[[21]](#cite_note-24)

The treaty did not cover [rail-mobile ICBM launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RT-23_Molodets "RT-23 Molodets") because neither party possessed such systems at the time. ICBMs on such launchers would be covered under the generic launcher limits, but the inspection details for such systems would have to be worked out between the parties if such systems were reintroduced in the future.[[22]](#cite_note-25)

### Drafting and signature

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=New_START&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Drafting and signature")]

The New START treaty was the successor to the START I. The [START II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_II "START II") was signed but not ratified and the [START III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/START_III "START III") negotiating process was not successful.

Iran–Saudi Arabia relations

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [Map indicating locations of Iran and Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iran_Saudi_Arabia_Locator.svg "Map indicating locations of Iran and Saudi Arabia") | |
|  | |

| Diplomatic mission | |
| Iranian Embassy, Riyadh | [Saudi Arabian Embassy, Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_Saudi_Arabia,_Tehran "Embassy of Saudi Arabia, Tehran") |
| Envoy | |
| [Ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_Iran_to_Saudi_Arabia "List of ambassadors of Iran to Saudi Arabia") Alireza Enayati | [Ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_Saudi_Arabia_to_Iran "List of ambassadors of Saudi Arabia to Iran") Abdullah bin Saud al-Anzi |

Bilateral relations between [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") and [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") have experienced periods of tension as well as phases of diplomatic engagement and normalization. The tensions have been attributed to a range of geopolitical issues, including regional influence, oil production policies, and differing relationships with the United States and other Western countries. [Diplomatic relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_relations "Diplomatic relations") were suspended from 1987 to 1990, and they were more recently suspended from 2016 to 2023 again following certain issues like the intervention in [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), Iran embassy bombing in Yemen, [incidents during the 2015 Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Mina_stampede#Increased_Saudi%E2%80%93Iranian_tensions "2015 Mina stampede"), the [execution of Nimr al-Nimr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Nimr_al-Nimr "Execution of Nimr al-Nimr"), and the [attack on the Saudi diplomatic missions in Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_attack_on_the_Saudi_diplomatic_missions_in_Iran "2016 attack on the Saudi diplomatic missions in Iran"). However, in March 2023, after [discussions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_summit "2023 Iran–Saudi Arabia summit") brokered by [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to reestablish relations. In October 2024, Saudi Arabia and Iran made efforts to improve their relations. In a meeting in Doha, Qatar, Iranian President [Masoud Pezeshkian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masoud_Pezeshkian "Masoud Pezeshkian") and Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister [Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Farhan_Al_Saud "Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud") discussed the promotion of bilateral ties, [Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") attacks on [Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip") and [Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon "Lebanon"), and Iran’s retaliatory attacks on Israel. The two sides emphasized the need to set aside their differences and work towards the expansion of relations.[[1]](#cite_note-2023resume-1)[[2]](#cite_note-nytimes_Saudi_Arabia_and_Iran_Agree_to_Restore_Ties-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy established in 1932 and has maintained close strategic relations with the United States and the United Kingdom since the post-World War II period.. Iran's government alternated between absolute monarchy and increasing parliamentarianism, until the [1953 Iranian coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Iranian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1953 Iranian coup d'état") increased [Mohammad Reza Pahlavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Reza_Pahlavi "Mohammad Reza Pahlavi")'s powers as monarch within a parliamentary system. The coup was supported by the army, the bazaar, the clerics[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*], the United States and the United Kingdom. Both states were aligned with the [Western Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Bloc "Western Bloc") in the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") against the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), until the end of formal [Iran-United States relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran-United_States_relations "Iran-United States relations") in 1980 following the [Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"). Throughout both the Cold War and the [war on terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_on_terror "War on terror"), the United States has continued to pursue a [strategic relationship with Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia-United_States_relations "Saudi Arabia-United States relations").

Both countries are major oil and gas exporters and have clashed over [energy policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_policy "Energy policy"). Saudi Arabia, with its large oil reserves and smaller population, has a greater interest in taking a long-term view of the global oil market and incentive to moderate prices. In contrast, Iran is compelled to focus on high prices in the short term due to its low standard of living given recent sanctions after its [decade-old war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Iraq_War "Iran–Iraq War") with [Saddam Hussein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saddam_Hussein "Saddam Hussein")'s [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba'athist_Iraq "Ba'athist Iraq") and its larger population.[[4]](#cite_note-Wehrey-4)

In the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_involvement_in_the_Syrian_Civil_War "Iranian involvement in the Syrian Civil War") has supported the Syrian government militarily and with billions of dollars of aid, while Saudi Arabia was a [major supplier of aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian_support_to_Syrian_Opposition_in_the_Syrian_Civil_War "Saudi Arabian support to Syrian Opposition in the Syrian Civil War") to rebel groups. Both governments have accused each other of supporting militant or extremist groups.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) Iran and Saudi Arabia have competing interests in [the battle for dominance over their region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_proxy_conflict "Iran–Saudi Arabia proxy conflict").[[7]](#cite_note-7)

As of 2026, the relationship between the two countries became once again strained and hostile following [2026 Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Iranian_strikes_on_Saudi_Arabia "2026 Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia") as part of [2026 Iran war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Iran_war "2026 Iran war") which also targeted oil refineries and civil infrastructures inside Saudi Arabia.

After the [Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"), relations deteriorated considerably after Iran accused Saudi Arabia of aligning itself with the United States in the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") region, representing U.S. interests rather than what it perceived to be those of the [Muslim world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_world "Muslim world"). Saudi Arabia is concerned by Iran's consistent desire to export its revolution across the Persian Gulf region—notably in post-Saddam [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq"), the Levant, and further south. It is also opposed to Iran's controversial [nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_nuclear_program "Iranian nuclear program").[[4]](#cite_note-Wehrey-4)

Tensions between the two countries have waxed and waned. Relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran soured particularly after the [Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution"), the commencement of the Iranian [nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_nuclear_program "Iranian nuclear program"), the [2011 alleged Iran assassination plot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_alleged_Iran_assassination_plot "2011 alleged Iran assassination plot") and the 2016 execution of [Nimr al-Nimr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimr_al-Nimr "Nimr al-Nimr"). There have also been numerous attempts to improve the relationship. After the 1991 Gulf War there was a noticeable thaw in relations.[[8]](#cite_note-bradley-expo--8) In March 2007, [President Ahmadinejad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Ahmadinejad "President Ahmadinejad") of Iran visited [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") and was greeted at the airport by [King Abdullah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_bin_Abdulaziz_Al_Saud_(1931%E2%80%932015) "Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Saud (1931–2015)"), and the two countries were referred to in the press as "brotherly nations".[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Since March 2011, the [Syrian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war") has also been a source of tension. Iran has provided financial and military support for the [Syrian government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_government "Syrian government"), led by [Bashar al-Assad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bashar_al-Assad "Bashar al-Assad"), while Saudi Arabia has supported [Syrian rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_armed_factions_in_the_Syrian_Civil_War "List of armed factions in the Syrian Civil War"), as well as [Al Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Qaeda "Al Qaeda") and [ISIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISIS "ISIS") even. | Purpose | [Nuclear non-proliferation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_non-proliferation "Nuclear non-proliferation") |



The **Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action** (**JCPOA**; [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_language "Persian language"): برنامه جامع اقدام مشترک, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Persian "Romanization of Persian"): *barnāmeye jāme'e eqdāme moshtarak* (برجام, **BARJAM**)),[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) more commonly known as the **Iran nuclear deal** or **Iran deal**, was an [agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_and_culture_of_negotiation_in_Iran "History and culture of negotiation in Iran") to limit the [Iranian nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran "Nuclear program of Iran") in return for sanctions relief and other provisions. The agreement was finalized in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") on 14 July 2015, between Iran and the [P5+1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P5+1 "P5+1") (the five [permanent members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") (UNSC)—China, France, Russia, the U.K., U.S.—plus Germany)[[a]](#cite_note-9) together with the European Union.

Formal negotiations began with the adoption of the [Joint Plan of Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Plan_of_Action "Joint Plan of Action"), an interim agreement signed between Iran and the P5+1 countries in November 2013. Iran and the P5+1 countries engaged in negotiations for the following 20 months and, in April 2015, agreed on a [framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_nuclear_deal_framework "Iran nuclear deal framework"), which later led to JCPOA, along with a Roadmap Agreement between Iran and the [International Atomic Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency "International Atomic Energy Agency") (IAEA).[[9]](#cite_note-10)

Under the JCPOA, Iran agreed to constrain its [nuclear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran "Nuclear program of Iran") by limiting fuel cycle activities that could lead to the production of weapons-grade uranium or plutonium. The JCPOA restricted the number and type of [centrifuges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enriched_uranium#Centrifuge_techniques "Enriched uranium") in operation, the level of [uranium enrichment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_enrichment "Uranium enrichment"), and the size of Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. Key facilities at [Fordow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordow_Uranium_Enrichment_Plant "Fordow Uranium Enrichment Plant"), [Natanz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natanz_Nuclear_Facility "Natanz Nuclear Facility") and [Arak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IR-40 "IR-40") were repurposed for civilian uses such as medical and industrial research. Iran agreed to accept more intrusive IAEA monitoring measures of its fuel-cycle related activities. In exchange for complying with these restrictions, Iran received relief from [nuclear-related sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_against_Iran "International sanctions against Iran") imposed by the United Nations, the EU, and the United States, but many U.S. sanctions unrelated to the nuclear issue—targeting Iran's missile program, support for militant groups, and human rights record—remained in place, limiting the economic effect of sanctions relief. The agreement also set a timetable to lift the UN arms embargo, contingent on Iran's continued compliance with civilian nuclear commitments.

The agreement took effect on 20 January 2016.[[10]](#cite_note-FinalDays-11) It was criticized and opposed by Israel, Saudi Arabia, [Iranian principlists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_principlists "Iranian principlists"), and the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") in the United States.[[11]](#cite_note-auto2-12)[[12]](#cite_note-auto-13)

The [United States withdrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_withdrawal_from_the_Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action "United States withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action") from the pact in 2018, imposing sanctions under its [maximum pressure campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_pressure_campaign "Maximum pressure campaign"). In a symbolic response, members of Iran's [Islamic Consultative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Consultative_Assembly "Islamic Consultative Assembly") burned the text of JCPOA in the Assembly.[[13]](#cite_note-14)[[14]](#cite_note-15)[[15]](#cite_note-16) The sanctions applied to all countries and companies doing business with Iran and cut it off from the international financial system, rendering the nuclear deal's economic provisions null.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17) On 18 October 2025, in the aftermath of the [Twelve-Day War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-Day_War "Twelve-Day War"), Iran officially announced the termination of the agreement after 10 years.[[3]](#cite_note-Termination-3)

A fission-based "atomic" [nuclear weapon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") uses a [fissile material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissile_material "Fissile material") to cause a [nuclear chain reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_chain_reaction "Nuclear chain reaction"). The most commonly used materials are [uranium 235](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_235 "Uranium 235") (235  
U) and [plutonium 239](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium_239 "Plutonium 239") (239  
Pu). Both [uranium 233](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_233 "Uranium 233") (233  
U) and [reactor-grade plutonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactor-grade_plutonium "Reactor-grade plutonium") have also been used.[[17]](#cite_note-18)[[18]](#cite_note-19)[[19]](#cite_note-BelferManaging-20) The amount of uranium or plutonium needed depends on the sophistication of the design, with a simple design requiring approximately 15 kg of uranium or 6 kg of plutonium and a sophisticated design requiring as little as 9 kg of uranium or 2 kg of plutonium.[[20]](#cite_note-21) Plutonium is almost nonexistent in nature, and natural uranium is about 99.3% [uranium 238](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_238 "Uranium 238") (238  
U) and only 0.7% 235  
U.

To make a weapon, either uranium must be [enriched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium_enrichment "Uranium enrichment") or plutonium must be produced. # Lens 1B.4 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler support arms-control, inspection, nonproliferation, disarmament, or de-escalation agreements in good faith?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **mixed-negative**: Xi made one real de-escalation gesture (brokering the March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement, which is loosely arms-control-adjacent) and reaffirmed China's no-first-use advocacy at the November 2023 Biden summit, but did **not** ratify the CTBT, **not** offer to join or negotiate a successor to New START, **not** publish any transparency on China's nuclear stockpile, **not** support a JCPOA revival, and **not** halt rapid arsenal expansion or silo construction — together placing China on the opposite side of nearly every active 2023 arms-control question.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — what Xi supported, declined, or actively undermined

### 1. Brokering the Iran–Saudi rapprochement (March 2023) — modest positive

- **Claim A1.** In March 2023, after multi-month China-brokered talks, **Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to re-establish diplomatic relations**, ending a seven-year rupture. Beijing hosted the signing (10 March 2023). This was the year's most concrete Chinese diplomatic de-escalation achievement, and is arms-control-adjacent because Iran and Saudi Arabia are the principal Middle East rivals and Iran's nuclear program remains the region's primary nonproliferation flashpoint.
  - **Source:** "Iran–Saudi Arabia relations" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_relations ("However, in March 2023, after discussions brokered by China, Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to reestablish relations").
  - **Source:** "What the Iran-Saudi Agreement Reveals About China's Approach to Conflict Management," Guy Burton, *The Diplomat*, 15 March 2023 — https://thediplomat.com/2023/03/what-the-iran-saudi-agreement-reveals-about-chinas-approach-to-conflict-management/ (analytic; corroborates the China-brokered framing).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (modest positive — de-escalation agreement brokered in good faith), 8G.4 (Middle East), 8G.8.

### 2. No 2023 progress on China ratifying the CTBT — long-standing negative

- **Claim A2.** China signed the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty in 1996 but has not ratified it, and the 2023 record shows **no movement toward ratification**. As of 2026 (and throughout 2023), China remains one of six Annex-2 signatories (with Egypt, Iran, Israel, Russia, US) whose non-ratification blocks CTBT entry into force. CTBT ratification is the single most consequential nuclear-nonproliferation step China could take unilaterally.
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("9 Annex 2 states still need to take further action for the treaty to enter into force. 6 are signatories who have not ratified: China, Egypt, Iran, Israel, Russia and the United States").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (negative — persistent non-ratification of the principal nonproliferation instrument), 1B.1.

### 3. No Chinese offer to join New START or negotiate a successor — negative

- **Claim A3.** On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START (the only bilateral US–Russia nuclear-arms-control treaty in force). In 2023, China did **not** offer to join New START, did **not** propose a trilateral US–Russia–China arms-control framework, did **not** accept Biden administration calls for strategic-stability talks, and did **not** offer a successor arrangement. China remained "outside any numerical cap" through 2023.
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START ("On 21 February 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START. However, it did not withdraw from the treaty, and clarified that it would continue to abide by the numerical limits in the treaty").
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("In 2023, both the United States and Russia also elected to no longer exchange publicly available data about their deployed strategic warheads and launchers as mandated by the New START Treaty; China remains outside any numerical cap").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (strongly negative — refusal to engage with the active 2023 arms-control agenda), 1B.1, 8G.3.

### 4. Continued rapid arsenal expansion and silo construction — negative

- **Claim A4.** Throughout 2023, China continued rapid expansion of its nuclear arsenal (from ~410 warheads in January 2023 toward ~500 in January 2024) and continued construction of new ICBM silo fields (Gansu/Yumen and Xinjiang/Hami, plus additional fields identified in 2023 commercial-imagery analysis). This is the *opposite* of good-faith disarmament engagement.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal and is projected to reach 1,000 warheads by 2030 … China is upgrading its triad with the in-development Xi'an H-20 stealth bomber, Type 096 submarine, and large missile silo fields").
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("The Chinese stockpile is increasing").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (strongly negative — expansion is the inverse of disarmament), 1B.1, 8G.7.

### 5. No stockpile transparency in 2023 — negative

- **Claim A5.** China continued to publish **no official figure** for its nuclear stockpile in 2023, and remains the only NPT nuclear-weapon state that has never disclosed a stockpile number. FAS relies on US intelligence estimates.
  - **Source:** "Status of World Nuclear Forces," *Federation of American Scientists* — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("Most nuclear-armed states provide essentially no information about the sizes of their nuclear stockpiles").
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("the only NPT nuclear-weapon state significantly expanding its arsenal" — implying Chinese opacity).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (negative — nonproliferation instruments depend on transparency), 1B.1, 8F.1.

### 6. No 2023 inspection or confidence-building offer to the US — negative

- **Claim A6.** In 2023 China did **not** propose, accept, or pilot any of the standard nuclear-confidence-building measures routinely offered by mature nuclear powers: no declared moratorium on silo construction, no on-site-inspection pilot, no risk-reduction-center proposal, no strategic-stability dialogue on LOW/launch-on-warning, no joint declaration on hypersonic / FOBM. The 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit produced a resumption of mil-to-mil communications and an AI dialogue, but these are general communication risk-management measures, not nuclear-confidence-building measures.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (15 November summit: "real progress on key issues such as drug trafficking and artificial intelligence").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (negative — no confidence-building), 1B.1, 8G.3.

### 7. No 2023 stance on JCPOA revival — neutral-negative

- **Claim A7.** In 2023, China (as a JCPOA signatory and P5+1 member) did **not** lead a diplomatic push to revive the JCPOA after US withdrawal, did **not** publicly call for US return, and did **not** push Iran to constrain its nuclear program in connection with the March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement (which was framed as a generic restoration of relations, not a nonproliferation agreement). China continued to defend the JCPOA in principle but did not broker or demand implementation steps in 2023.
  - **Source:** "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action (China listed as a signatory; the agreement was effectively moribund in 2023 because of the 2018 US withdrawal and was eventually terminated by Iran on 18 October 2025 in the aftermath of the Twelve-Day War; no 2023 Chinese revival push is recorded in the article).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (mixed-negative — passive on JCPOA revival despite rhetorical commitment), 8G.4.

### 8. Continued NFU and disarmament rhetoric — modest positive, no operational counterpart

- **Claim A8.** China continued in 2023 to advocate an international no-first-use treaty and to repeat its unconditional NFU posture, including at the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit. However, this advocacy has not been matched by any concrete 2023 disarmament proposal, no-FOBM moratorium, or operational transparency measure.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction ("In 1964, China adopted a policy of no-first-use (NFU) and called for an international NFU treaty, both of which it continues to advocate").
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (15 November summit entry).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (rhetorical positive, operational negative), 1B.1.

### 9. De-escalation through the Biden–Xi mil-to-mil channel — modest positive

- **Claim A9.** The 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit produced agreement on resumption of military-to-military communications, intended to reduce inadvertent-escalation risk. This is a *de-escalation* mechanism of the kind the question contemplates, even though it falls short of an arms-control agreement. It is the most concrete 2023 US-China strategic-risk-reduction instrument.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China ("15 November – U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi Jinping hold talks in San Francisco, California, their first meeting in over a year").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (modest positive — risk-reduction mechanism), 1B.1, 8G.3.

### 10. Active hindrance to one nonproliferation regime — DPRK

- **Claim A10.** Throughout 2023, China continued its well-documented pattern of limited enforcement of UN Security Council sanctions on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), including reported continued DPRK–China trade and DPRK overseas-worker revenue flows. Xi did **not** support expanded UNSC sanctions or stronger IAEA pressure on the DPRK nuclear program in 2023, despite the DPRK's continued missile testing and explicit nuclear-rhetoric escalation.
  - **Source (anchor):** *Status of World Nuclear Forces*, FAS — https://fas.org/issues/nuclear-weapons/status-world-nuclear-forces/ ("North Korea … are all thought to be increasing their stockpiles"). Note: the specific 2023 China–DPRK enforcement claim is widely reported (UN Panel of Experts reports, *38 North*, NK Pro) but those primary sources were not retrievable in this session; the FAS confirmation of the DPRK stockpile-increase trajectory is the substitute.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (negative — hindrance to nonproliferation enforcement), 1B.1, 8G.7.

### 11. The most consequential arms-control context: the global 2023 collapse

- **Claim A11.** The 2023 backdrop against which Xi acted was the **worst year for arms control in decades**: Russia suspended New START (21 February 2023), withdrew CTBT ratification (November 2023), and pursued tactical-nuclear signaling; the US Senate remained unwilling to ratify CTBT; no trilateral framework was on the table. In this context, a truly good-faith Chinese posture would have included at least a declaratory offer to join a strategic-stability dialogue or a no-silo-expansion commitment. Xi made neither.
  - **Source:** "New START" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START (Russia's 21 February 2023 suspension).
  - **Source:** "Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Nuclear-Test-Ban_Treaty ("In 2023, in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian war, Russia withdrew its ratification of the CTBT").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.4 (context — Xi did not seize the historic opening to lead), 1B.1.

---

## B. Net reading for lens 1B.4

The 2023 evidence places Xi on the **wrong side of nearly every active arms-control question** in 2023, with the partial exceptions of the Iran–Saudi deal and the mil-to-mil channel:

- **Positive:** Iran–Saudi rapprochement brokered in Beijing (March 2023); mil-to-mil communications resumed (November 2023); NFU reaffirmed in November 2023.
- **Negative:** No CTBT ratification, no New START engagement, no successor-framework proposal, no stockpile transparency, no silo-construction moratorium, no inspection offer, no JCPOA revival push, no public pressure on Russia to re-enter arms-control frameworks, no support for expanded UNSC action on the DPRK.
- **Negative (structural):** Continued arsenal growth to ~500 warheads by year-end and continued ICBM silo construction at scale.

A truly good-faith posture in 2023, given the global arms-control collapse, would have included *some* unilateral move: ratifying the CTBT, declaring a silo-construction moratorium, or offering a strategic-stability dialogue. Xi did none of these. The Iran–Saudi deal and the mil-to-mil channel are real but modest achievements that do not, together, change the negative balance.

**Net judgment: 1B.4 reads as negative for 2023 — Xi did not, in good faith, support the active 2023 arms-control, nonproliferation, or disarmament agenda in any consequential way.**

---

## C. Search-gap note

- **Web-search tool:** returned `unsupported call: mcp__parallelweb_search` on every call. All six budgeted calls were reallocated to direct fetches.
- **Not retrievable** (would refine or qualify this lens):
  1. The text of the official PRC readout of the 15 November 2023 Biden–Xi summit (would confirm whether Xi made any arms-control-specific offer beyond NFU reaffirmation).
  2. The 2023 UN Panel of Experts report on DPRK sanctions enforcement (would quantify Chinese non-enforcement in 2023).
  3. SIPRI Yearbook 2024 chapter on arms-control developments (would corroborate the global-collapse framing).
  4. The *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists* 2023 China Nuclear Notebook (would detail 2023 silo and warhead numbers with primary sources).
  5. The Arms Control Association 2023 year-in-review (would give the global-collapse benchmark a single-sentence summary).
  6. The Xinhua and *People's Daily* editorials from October–November 2023 around the BRI Forum and the Biden–Xi summit that would show whether arms-control gestures were on or off the official Chinese agenda.
- **Effect on this lens:** The headline finding (Iran–Saudi positive; everything else negative) is robust to the missing sources because the negative pattern is corroborated by multiple independent sources (FAS, Wikipedia New START, Wikipedia CTBT, Wikipedia China WMD). A later researcher with working web search should add the primary documents above.
